title: Why I Ditched a Custom App and Moved All Customer Notifications to Telegram
summary: Moving from custom support apps to Telegram improves notification reliability for ecommerce sellers. Self-built apps suffer from delayed push notifications, silent channels, and high maintenance costs, whereas Telegram's independent infrastructure ensures messages arrive promptly even when the app restarts.
content:
If you run a Shopify or WooCommerce store, you know the pain of missing a customer message. You might blame your network, or your response speed. But often, the real culprit is the self-built support app you are using.
Most ecommerce helpdesks offer a dedicated mobile app. It looks professional. But there is an open secret in the SaaS world: most small to mid-sized self-built apps have unreliable push notifications.
Why do self-built support apps fail?

Delays: System push channels batch notifications to save battery. Customer messages get queued behind. By the time you see it, the customer is gone.
Silent channels: When the app is killed, the push channel breaks. You miss messages until you manually reopen the app.
High maintenance: Every iOS/Android update can break the push logic. Maintenance costs get passed to you.
Why Telegram is different
It's not tied to the system push policy. No merged notifications. No rate-limiting in the same way. If the app gets woken up, the message arrives.
What this means for sellers
The takeaway
Don't let an app icon fool you. Reliability is the real standard.

title: Understanding AI Agent Architecture - Part 1
summary: AI agents combine language models with tools, resources, and feedback loops to achieve autonomy that LLMs alone cannot. Agent architecture can be designed using finite state machines or hierarchical state machines, with tools, memory, and observability as essential components.
content:
I'm currently reading AI Agents: The Definitive Guide by Nicole Koenigstein for a book club. In an effort to solidify my learnings and get the most out of the book, I'm noting things that stand out to me as I read through each chapter. Maybe this can also provide some quick knowledge to someone else who's interested in learning about AI agents :)
1. An AI agent is a model that "sits in a loop of reasoning, acting and feedback... A language model on its own is like a developer cut off from resources such as Stack Overflow, IDEs, or Github". This is why agents are so important - they use an LLM while providing the infrastructure of tools, resources, and looping it needs to become autonomous and helpful. LLMs alone are limited in their capabilities and output.
2. The design of agents can be represented as finite state machines (FSMs) and hierarchical state machines (HSMs). The book dives into the differences between the two in order to demonstrate the concept of agent architecture. A finite state machine "describes the modes your system can be in and the allowed transitions between them", representing a simpler architecture for single step to state mappings. HSMs, on the other hand, "let states contain other states". Hierarchical state machines allow for breaking down complex processes into many nodes but still encapsulating them as a single state. This is further demonstrated in code through LangGraph's representation of agents as subgraphs. More complex tool calling agents/multi-agent systems can be designed using HSMs. FSMs and HSMs provide "the conceptual foundation for agent design".
3. Tools, memory, and observability are important parts of an agent system. With LangChain, tools can be defined with the @tool decorator and bound to an agent. Memory can be saved so that the context isn't lost after each agent run. In LangGraph, agent state can be a TypedDict that keeps previous messages in a common structure for a current execution. A webhook can be attached to a Workflow Rule as an instant action to post data to another system, for example a won deal to an internal tool. Zoho states daily webhook limits that depend on your edition.
Custom Functions are written in Deluge Script and attached to a Workflow Rule as an instant action. title: Phones on shelves got 15% pricier in 2026: how memory chips broke the price curve
summary: Smartphone prices increased 15% on average in 2026 as memory chip costs quadrupled since late 2025, breaking the historical price-decline curve. Manufacturers responded by raising prices on existing models, increasing new launch costs, and reducing storage and camera specs.
content:
Phones that were already on shelves went up in price by 15% on average in 2026, and some models nearly doubled. That is from Counterpoint Research's Global Smartphone Price Increase Tracker, published on 3 September 2026, and the cause it names is memory: prices for the chips that hold your apps and photos have risen fourfold since Q4 2025.
If you have spent years watching last year's flagship get cheaper every month, this breaks the rule you learned. Here is how a part you never see ends up on the price tag.
Normally a phone launches at its highest price and drifts down. The parts inside it get cheaper as factories improve, and the maker can cut the price and still keep its margin.
That only works while the bill of materials goes down. In a phone, two big lines on that bill are DRAM (the working memory) and NAND flash (the storage). When those two jump, the maker of a phone that is already on sale has three options: eat the cost, raise the price, or quietly ship less memory in the next batch.
According to Counterpoint, they did all three. Over 40% of smartphone models had a price increase so far in 2026, which the firm calls a first for the industry. New launches were 25% more expensive than the models they replaced a year earlier. And makers started trimming specs: "lower storage capacities, reduced camera configurations and the reintroduction of 4G models in select price segments."
The warning signs were there in January. Counterpoint's Q4 2025 market report said the average selling price had passed $400 in a single quarter for the first time, up 8% year on year, with "higher Bill of Materials (BOM) costs" and "the ongoing memory shortages" in the mix. Research Director Tarun Pathak expected a "continued rise in ASPs supported by ... DRAM/NAND price hikes." That was the forecast. The September tracker is what it looked like in shops.

title: Kubernetes Pod Churn & Node Thrashing: Ephemeral Storage Exhaustion and Eviction Cascades
summary: Unbounded ephemeral storage in Kubernetes worker pods causes disk pressure cascades that trigger aggressive pod eviction, cluster auto-scaler thrashing, and budget overruns. Proper ephemeral storage requests and limits prevent this failure mode in high-throughput microservice systems.
content:
When background worker pods continuously write temporary scratch files, un-rotated log buffers, or dynamic assets directly to container filesystems without explicit ephemeral storage limits, worker nodes quietly enter local disk pressure states. The kubelet then triggers aggressive pod evictions, sparking cluster-wide pod churn, Karpenter/Cluster Autoscaler thrashing, and AWS bill inflation. Here is an architectural deep dive into diagnosing local disk exhaustion and configuring resilient kubelet eviction boundaries.
In high-throughput B2B SaaS platforms running containerized microservices, background processing workloads (e.g., generating PDF reports, processing video/image assets, compiling code, or handling CSV batch imports) frequently rely on local container file systems for temporary scratch space. Under heavy traffic, un-capped ephemeral storage usage creates an invisible cluster-level failure mode: Cascading Node Eviction and Auto-Scaler Thrashing.
By default, when a container writes files to its own filesystem (outside of explicitly mounted Persistent Volumes), those writes land on the node's local disk through the container runtime's writable layer, typically the OverlayFS storage driver. Disk-backed emptyDir volumes and container logs consume the same node disk. If a pod uses significant local disk space without ephemeral storage requests and limits in its manifest, it triggers a chain reaction across the host node.
Unbounded Disk Growth: A burst of PDF generation worker tasks writes 15GB of temporary files to /tmp inside the container overlay filesystem.
Kubelet Disk Pressure Breach: The node's disk crosses a kubelet hard eviction threshold (by default, nodefs.available below 10% or imagefs.available below 15%). The kubelet marks the node DiskPressure = True, the node is tainted, and the scheduler stops placing new pods on it.

title: 733,203 attestations were taken back
summary: Analysis of Ethereum Attestation Service finds 733,203 revoked attestations (15% of all attestations), primarily from one Coinbase issuer revoking its own verifications. Self-correction through revocation is ordinary operational work at scale, with no dispute mechanism available.
content:
733,203 attestations were taken back. Every single one by the party that wrote it.
I went counting because someone told me, politely and correctly, that a signature does not make a statement true. I had no good answer, so I went looking for what the ecosystem does when a signed statement stops holding.
The numbers, taken against the three EAS indexers rather than estimated:
Base: 678,895 revoked of 3,651,900 attestations
Optimism: 54,213 of 1,319,189
Ethereum mainnet: 95 of 14,956
That is 733,203 of 4,986,045, so a headline near 15 percent. The headline is the least useful part.
On Base, three schemas carry 97 percent of all revocations, and all three belong to one issuer: verifiedAccount (723,600 issued, 409,490 revoked), verifiedCountry (307,123 issued, 144,207 revoked), verifiedCoinbaseOne (189,434 issued, 103,295 revoked). An exchange revoking roughly half of its own verifications, continuously.
Anyone can reproduce it:
curl -s https://base.easscan.org/graphql -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"query":"{ aggregateAttestation(where: {revoked: {equals: true}}) { _count { id } } }"}'

and groupByAttestation(by: [schemaId], where: {revoked: {equals: true}}) for the breakdown. One warning if you repeat it: during my run the Base endpoint returned a maintenance page with a 200 status for a valid query. That reads as a zero unless you look at the body.
What I expected to find, and did not
I expected to find disputes. A registry full of signed statements, some of them wrong, and a trail of parties contesting each other.
There are no disputes, because there is no such operation. A revocation is the issuer withdrawing its own statement. All 733,203 of them. The counterparty has no move at all.
That reframes the whole picture. The need to revise a signed record is not theoretical and not rare: it is ordinary operational work at a scale of hundreds of thousands. And the only tool available is self-correction.

Flutter + Physical AI: Release Checklist for Performance, Safety, and Reliability


A production release connecting Flutter to smart glasses, Jetson, ROS 2, and AI models needs more than a smooth demo. Review latency, stale data, degraded modes, privacy, and recovery.
Run sustained tests on supported devices. Record p95/p99 frame timings, source-to-display age, memory growth, dropped updates, and reconnect time.
Cover network loss, gateway restarts, unavailable model capabilities, permission revocation, low memory, thermal throttling, and stale telemetry.
Ensure important commands have IDs, authorization, acknowledgement, timeout, and reconciliation behavior. Distinguish unknown outcomes from confirmed failures.
Ensure logs are useful without exposing raw media, secrets, or unnecessary personal data. Correlate client and gateway diagnostics.
Document supported device/model combinations, performance baseline, and thresholds that trigger rollback. Monitor regressions after rollout.

title: Stop Guessing Your RAG Chunking Strategy. Inspect It
summary: The AabiTech RAG Chunking Simulator helps developers experiment with different chunking strategies for RAG pipelines by comparing approaches, visualizing chunk boundaries, and measuring trade-offs—all running locally in the browser for privacy. The tool enables developers to inspect chunking behavior and understand configuration tradeoffs before integrating them into production pipelines.
content:
If you've built a RAG pipeline, you know chunking isn't just splitting text into smaller pieces.
Chunk size affects context retention. Overlap introduces duplication. Splitting on arbitrary boundaries can separate code, paragraphs, or related ideas. And a configuration that looks reasonable on paper might perform poorly during retrieval.
Usually, figuring this out means tweaking parameters, rerunning scripts, dumping chunks to the console, and comparing outputs manually.
I built a tool to make that workflow easier.
Meet the "AabiTech RAG Chunking Simulator" (https://aabitech.com/tools/rag-chunking-simulator) — an interactive workspace for experimenting with chunking strategies before integrating them into your RAG pipeline.
What you can do
Compare strategies: Experiment with fixed-size, recursive, sentence-aware, paragraph-aware, Markdown-aware, and other splitting approaches.
Inspect boundaries: Visualize how source text is divided and examine individual chunks and overlapping regions.
Measure trade-offs: Review chunk counts, size distributions, overlap, and estimated token and embedding costs.
Explore retrieval: Test lightweight keyword retrieval, parent-child chunking, and context-window budgets.
Export your results: Download chunks in JSON, JSONL, CSV, or text formats, and generate Python splitter examples for supported frameworks.
Save experiments: Keep configuration snapshots in your browser or share settings through URL hashes.
Built with privacy in mind
The chunking engine processes your source text locally in the browser instead of sending it to a dedicated chunking API.
That makes it useful for experimenting with documentation, code snippets, and sample datasets without unnecessarily uploading them elsewhere.
What it's useful for
This isn't a replacement for evaluating retrieval quality against your real dataset. It's a way to inspect chunking behavior, understand configuration trade-offs, and narrow down the settings worth testing in your actual pipeline.

title: The 44% Problem
summary: While AI was involved in 84% of ransomware attacks, the critical finding is that 44% of victims were compromised through their own AI agents—meaning attackers exploited internal systems rather than external networks. The article frames this as a proof problem: organizations lack visibility into AI agent decisions and authorization trails, creating an unauditable security gap that favors attackers.
content:
October 15, 2026
The report says AI was involved in 84% of ransomware attacks. That number is being repeated everywhere today. It is not the important one.
The important number is 44%.
Forty-four percent of victims reported that the attack exploited their own AI agents. Not an attacker's AI. Not a malicious model. Their own systems, running with their own credentials, doing what they were built to do—except the agent had been manipulated, or the credentials had been harvested, or the authority had been misrepresented.
The attack did not come from outside. It came from inside the trust boundary.
When an organization deploys an AI agent, it grants that agent authority. The authority to read records. To call APIs. To move data. To execute actions. The agent acts under delegated permissions, using credentials the organization issued, performing tasks the organization defined.
Every one of those actions is a decision. The agent decides what to read, what to call, what to execute. In most organizations, no one can prove what the agent decided. No one can verify the authority that permitted it. No one can replay the sequence.
The 44% figure is the consequence. When attackers compromise an agent, they inherit its authority. When they manipulate its inputs, they manipulate its decisions. When they harvest its credentials, they act as the agent.
And when the breach is discovered, there is nothing to examine. There is no record of the decision. There is no proof of the authority. There is no replay of the sequence.
The investigation starts from zero.
The report does not say AI caused the attacks. It says AI was involved. The distinction matters because the industry is responding to the wrong half.
The offensive use of AI—writing code, scanning for weaknesses, automating intrusion—is a threat problem. It belongs to the defenders. It is not solved by a standard.

title: Entra Seamless SSO Not Working: A Read-First Intranet Zone, Kerberos Ticket, and AZUREADSSOACC Triage
summary: This technical guide diagnoses Microsoft Entra Seamless SSO failures by walking through the chain of dependencies (device authentication, browser zone settings, domain controller communication, ticket encryption) that must all hold for SSO to work. It addresses common misdiagnoses and recent breakage from 2026 domain controller patches that changed encryption defaults for Azure AD SSO accounts.
content:
Helpdesk: "Outlook on the web used to just open on my desk PC. Now it asks for my password every morning." A second ticket from the same floor: the sign-in page takes the username, pauses, then wants a password, and only for people on the older domain-joined laptops. Someone has already proposed "turn Seamless SSO off and on again," running the key rollover a second time to be safe, or adding autologon.microsoftazuread-sso.com to Trusted sites for everyone.
Don't reset anything yet. Microsoft Entra Seamless SSO is opportunistic: when any link fails, the user silently falls back to a normal password prompt, so the only symptom is "it asks for my password." It only works when the whole chain holds: the device actually uses Seamless SSO (not PRT-based SSO) → the feature is enabled on the tenant for this user's AD forest → the browser or Office client treats https://autologon.microsoftazuread-sso.com as Local intranet and is allowed to send Kerberos to it → the device can reach a domain controller with a sane clock and gets a ticket for the AZUREADSSOACC computer account → that ticket is small enough and encrypted with a key Microsoft Entra ID still holds → Entra ID can map the ticket's SID to a synced cloud user. In 2026 a new link fails more often than it used to: domain controllers patched in April and July 2026 stop assuming RC4 for accounts without an explicit encryption type, and Microsoft calls out the AzureADSSOAcc$ account by name.
If the device is Windows 10 or 11 and Microsoft Entra hybrid joined, Seamless SSO isn't what signs the user in at all. Microsoft says SSO on hybrid joined, Entra joined, and registered devices runs on the Primary Refresh Token, so start with the AzureAdPrt: NO triage or the Hybrid Azure AD join pending triage. Every freelance developer and boutique agency owner knows the dreaded Friday afternoon Slack message that starts with four seemingly innocent words:

Behind those five words usually hides 14 to 20 hours of uncontracted architectural work—a "lightweight" role-based admin panel, an extra Stripe webhook flow, or dark-mode theming across 12 screens. 
Freelancers face a painful dilemma:
Eat the hours and watch your effective hourly rate plummet.
Push back awkwardly and risk sounding defensive or damaging a warm client relationship.
ScopeGuard is a $19/month micro-SaaS and contract shield built for independent developers, designers, and consultants. Freelancers and agencies sign strict Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs). Pasting a client's proprietary FinTech architecture, hourly rates, and signed SOW clauses into a third-party cloud API violates enterprise confidentiality clauses. By running open-weight Google Gemma 3 4B locally (or on an isolated private instance), zero bytes of client IP ever leave your infrastructure.

content:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle
You run docker compose up. The API container dies. You get forty lines of noise, paste them into a chatbot, and get back a confident paragraph — sometimes quoting an error line that was never in your log.
CrashCart is a debugging assistant that has to show its receipts. You paste a terminal log, stack trace, or build failure, and CrashCart:
Redacts secrets in your browser — API keys, tokens, passwords in connection strings, private keys — and shows you exactly what will be sent.
Asks Gemma 4, an open-weight model, for a structured diagnosis.
Checks every line the model quotes against your actual log. Quotes it finds get real line numbers and are highlighted in context. Quotes it can't find are flagged ⚠ and set aside. If none of the evidence checks out, CrashCart lowers the confidence itself — and shows you what the model originally claimed.
DEMO:

Every result is split three ways. You also get the smallest safe fix with copyable commands, steps to check that it worked, warnings on risky commands like rm -rf or --legacy-peer-deps (from fixed rules, not the model), a ready-to-paste GitHub issue, and a Markdown report. CrashCart never runs commands, never edits your code, and stores nothing.
Freelance web developers. They bill by the hour, debug stacks they didn't set up across several client projects, and regularly have to explain a failure to a client or another developer — that's what the issue draft and report are for. They're also the people most uneasy about pasting client logs into someone else's AI, which is exactly where open weights come in (more below).

title: I Ran `npm fund` and Found 47 Packages Keeping My App Alive
summary: Investigating npm fund reveals that critical packages like chalk—downloaded billions of times weekly—are maintained by just two people and remain vulnerable to targeted phishing attacks, as evidenced by a 2025 compromise that spread malicious versions to 99% of cloud environments. The article highlights funding and security gaps when high-impact infrastructure depends on small volunteer teams.
content:
I've been seeing the same line at the bottom of every npm install for years:
added 47 packages, and 12 packages are looking for funding
  run `npm fund` for details

I've never once run that command. It felt like a nag — the software equivalent of "did you mean to donate?" So last week, out of pure curiosity, I typed it.
What I got was a tree. Not a guilt trip, not a paywall — just a list of 12 packages I use every single day, each with a link to the human being who keeps it alive. Most of them I'd never heard of. A few I'd been taking for granted my entire career.
I picked five to look into. Here's what I found.
chalk is the package that colors your terminal output. If you've ever seen a green "success" or a red "error" in a CLI tool, there's a good chance chalk did that. It's maintained by Sindre Sorhus and Josh Junon, and it's downloaded billions of times a week.

content:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle
Lots of people run a side hustle that's really a small rental business: a duplex, a basement unit, a few doors bought one at a time. The paperwork that bites them isn't the mortgage. It's the lease. When does the renewal or rent-change notice have to go out? On what day does a late fee actually start, and how big can it get? When is the deposit refund due after move-out?
Lease Lens takes a pile of residential leases and gives you, for each one:
the key dates: term, last day to send the renewal/rent-change notice (plus a reminder two weeks before), and the deposit-return deadline (business days handled);
a late-fee table for 1 to 30 days late (grace period, flat or percent fee, daily fee "thereafter", monthly cap);
a state check of the late-fee terms for Colorado, New York and Texas;
an .ics calendar to import into Google/Outlook/Apple Calendar, and a leases.csv row per lease that pastes into a renewal tracker;
a field-by-field audit: every value next to the exact lease sentence it came from, marked ok, FIXED or CHECK.
Who pays for this? Property managers and small landlords who take over a building with existing leases already pay someone (or give up an evening) to pull these terms out by hand. It's called lease abstraction. Our plan is to keep the CLI free and open, and charge for the packaged pieces around it: we already sell a $12 Lease Renewal Tracker spreadsheet whose Leases tab uses the same columns as leases.csv.

This is a real run on an 8-core CPU with no GPU: about 29 seconds per lease. The GIF speeds up the model wait 6x (MP4). Real output files are in examples/.

You start with your labor rate and your parts costs. Supplier raised prices? Import a CSV or apply a bulk percent change, preview what moves, then save. Techs only ever see sell prices. Your costs stay private.
On site, the tech builds a proposal with up to four options from the price book, marks the one they recommend and adds optional extras. Then they hand over the phone or tablet. The homeowner sees the options side by side, picks one, adds any extras and signs on the screen. Or the shop sends a secure link and they sign later.
Once it's signed, the proposal locks and the shop gets a signed PDF. No "that's not what you told me" later.
Approved proposal? There's a Create invoice button right on it. The invoice carries the approved work over, goes out as a branded PDF, and you mark it paid when the money comes in. TierMenu records payments but doesn't process cards, so shops keep whatever they already use to get paid.

title: Why "discipline" won't save you from tutorial hell (and why it's a calendar math problem)
summary: Online courses often fail not due to lack of discipline but because developers underestimate the actual time required—one hour of video typically demands four hours of total work when accounting for setup, debugging, and context-switching. A 40-hour course becomes a 160-hour commitment that few can sustain alongside full-time work over seven months.
content:
Whenever someone confesses that they bought another 40-hour course and abandoned it by module 3, the standard response is almost always moralizing: "You just need more discipline. Wake up at 5 AM. Grind harder."
This advice completely misses the point. You don’t have a willpower problem—you have a simple calendar math problem. Here is the arithmetic that online course creators never show you.
The Fallacy of the 40-Hour Course
When you buy a "40-hour comprehensive bootcamp" on Udemy or Coursera, you do some quick mental math: 40 hours of video, studying 1 hour a day, finished in 40 days. Totally doable.
Except in real life, software development has a brutal multiplier effect. One hour of video usually requires an hour of typing along, another hour of debugging environment and dependency errors, plus the mental tax of context-switching after a tiring day job.
In reality, one hour of video easily demands four hours of real work. That 40-hour course is actually a 160-hour project.
The Calendar Reality: The Denominator Never Changes
Now look at your actual calendar. On paper, your weekends are wide open. In reality, you have a day job, errands, commute, relationships, and basic cognitive fatigue. On an average week, you can realistically protect maybe 5 to 8 interrupted evening hours.
Now run the math: 160 required hours divided by 6 hours a week equals 26 weeks. That is nearly seven months of flawless, uninterrupted consistency just to reach the end of one beginner tutorial.
During those seven months, your company changes priorities, a shiny new framework drops on Twitter, or you get sick for a week. The moment life interrupts you for 10 days, your mental context evaporates. You look at module 18, feel completely lost, blame your "lack of discipline," and start looking for an easier roadmap.
Discipline cannot solve an equation where the numerator is 160 hours and the denominator is 6.

title: The AI agent kill switch is a procedure, not a feature
summary: An AI agent kill switch must be a documented operational procedure with measurable outcomes, not merely disabling a credential, as agents may still access stored keys, write files, or continue executing background jobs. Effective containment requires identifying all action paths and assigning independent authority to stop each.
content:
An invoice-processing agent starts submitting the same job repeatedly. You disable its principal. Even if Microsoft Graph now rejects its requests, the agent may still use a provider key, write export files or leave accepted jobs running.
Which effects did the kill switch actually stop? The credential operation may have succeeded without containing the workload.
An AI agent kill switch is an operational procedure with a testable outcome.
The hypothetical invoice agent has four action paths: Graph access, model access, local writes and submitted jobs. Following those paths exposes the architectural obligation: someone outside the agent must retain the authority and information needed to stop its consequential activity.
"Stop" needs a defined outcome. Containment denies specified consequential actions; quiescence additionally requires relevant execution and outstanding work to reach verified terminal states. A paused or queued job is not terminal, and completed work may still have produced effects requiring recovery.
The invoice incident requires both: no further submissions or export writes, no remaining agent execution and no unresolved processing jobs. A lower-risk incident might permit isolated computation to continue while denying every forbidden effect.
Three artifacts make that objective reviewable. The stop scope identifies effects, execution units and permitted collateral impact. The shutdown protocol assigns independent authority, dependencies and failure handling. The acceptance report records observed coverage, timing and persistence.
Build the scope from credentials, reachable destinations, writable resources and submitted work. "All registered paths are closed" is a bounded claim; "the agent cannot cause harm" is not. Every new tool integration should identify both the authority it adds and how that authority will be withdrawn.

title: Google Was Spending 52% of Its Crawl on Dead URLs. Here's Our Audit and Fix.
summary: A website audit revealed that 52% of Google's crawl budget over 90 days was spent on non-existent URLs left over from a prior security breach, including fake API endpoints, WordPress artifacts, and injected page names. The fix involved identifying and removing the dead URLs rather than redirecting them, freeing crawl budget for new page discovery.
content:
Our new pages were indexing slowly, and everything obvious checked out: 64/64 pages returning 200, self-referencing canonicals, a valid sitemap, no broken internal links. So we stopped guessing and opened the one report most site owners never look at: Google Search Console → Settings → Crawl stats.
It took about five minutes to find the problem.
Over the last 90 days, Google made 546 crawl requests to our site — roughly six a day. The average response time was 370 ms, which is fine. Speed was not the bottleneck.
The response breakdown was:
Not found (404): 52%
OK (200): 44%
Not modified (304): 2%
Moved permanently (301): 2%
And by purpose: 93% refresh (re-checking pages Google already knows) against 7% discovery (finding new ones). More than half of a very small crawl budget was being spent on URLs that no longer exist, while new pages waited for discovery that barely happened.
The crawl-stats drilldown lists example URLs. Ours fell into three groups, all leftovers from a period when the site was compromised, before we rebuilt and locked it down:
Parasite endpoints — /api/stock/check.php, /api/cart/get-simple.php and friends, from a fake e-commerce layer that once lived on the domain. These alone accounted for dozens of requests.
WordPress leftovers — /feed/, /comments/feed/, an old /wp-content/uploads/ image path. Our site is hand-built static HTML; there is no WordPress anywhere in the stack. Google was still testing those paths months later.
Injected page names — random 12345678.shtml files that existed briefly during the compromise and never again.
Every one of them correctly returns 404. The failure wasn't the responses — it was that Google kept spending requests on them.
No redirecting the junk to the homepage. Mass redirects of unrelated dead URLs are treated as soft 404s and can create new problems. A dead parasite URL deserves a clean death, not a redirect.

title: Web Security Basics: 9 Practical Steps to Protect Your Website
summary: Website security requires practical measures including regular software updates, strong password management with multi-factor authentication, HTTPS encryption, and removing unused extensions to reduce attack surface. Web Security Basics: 9 Practical Steps to Protect Your Website


Website security is not just a concern for large companies. Personal blogs, small business websites, online magazines, and independent projects can all become targets of automated attacks, compromised passwords, outdated software, and poorly configured services.
The good news is that several practical measures can significantly improve a website's security. Although no checklist can eliminate every risk, establishing strong security habits helps reduce common vulnerabilities and makes recovery easier when something goes wrong.
Outdated software is one of the most avoidable sources of website risk.
Content management systems, themes, plugins, frameworks, and server components may receive updates that fix security vulnerabilities. Delaying these updates can leave known weaknesses exposed.
A sensible maintenance routine includes:
Updating the core platform and dependencies.
Removing unused themes, extensions, and packages.
Reviewing security advisories for important dependencies.
Testing significant updates before applying them to critical production systems.
Updates should be performed carefully, particularly on websites that depend on many extensions. A backup and a simple rollback plan can reduce the risk of unexpected downtime.
Weak or reused passwords can allow attackers to gain access to administrative accounts.
Use unique passwords for important accounts and store them in a reputable password manager. Enable multifactor authentication whenever it is supported, especially for hosting dashboards, administrator accounts, and domain registrars.
For websites with multiple administrators, assign individual accounts instead of sharing a single login. This makes access easier to manage and helps establish accountability.
If an administrator no longer needs access, remove or disable the account promptly.

title: Node.js API Routes and Server Actions: 3 Error Tracking Boundaries (With Attribution)
summary: Effective error tracking requires a stable application contract capturing both exception details and cost-attribution context (release, environment, pricing rule, cost center) before choosing an error backend. This decouples pricing logic from monitoring provider changes while maintaining support team usability.
content:
Instrument three server-side boundaries, but define the cost-attribution record before choosing the error backend. For a customer-support pricing rule behind a flag, that means one normalized exception contract across Next.js route handlers, server actions, and background jobs, with release, environment, pricingRule, and costCenter attached at capture time.
TL;DR: a capture-and-lookup service is enough when the job is grouping server exceptions and feeding an internal support view. It is not enough for browser source maps, alert delivery, distributed trace exploration, replay, or proof that a scheduled job ran. Keep the application contract stable so the provider behind it can move without edits to pricing logic.
Start from the support question: why did this account receive the wrong quote? A stack trace locates the failed code. It does not identify the rule, deployment, environment, or owning budget. Those are application facts, so the application has to supply them.
I would keep eight fields. Four describe the exception: name, message, stack, and occurredAt. Four make it actionable: release, environment, pricingRule, and costCenter. A ninth field, boundary, separates synchronous request work from deferred work. The shape is deliberately small because every extra dimension becomes a privacy decision, a grouping hazard, and another thing an SDK migration must preserve.
Headers need even less enthusiasm. Copying the full request header map is quick, but it can pull cookies and authorization credentials into an error store. For this workflow, allowlist content-type, user-agent, and x-request-id. Three headers. No clever redaction regex.
The attribution rule is equally plain: costCenter names the team paying for and operating the pricing action; pricingRule names the versioned business decision. Neither field should be derived from an exception message. Messages change. Identifiers should not.

title: Lock GitHub Actions dependencies to reviewed commits with workflow lockfiles
summary: GitHub Actions Workflow Lockfiles, now in public preview, pin exact commits for direct, transitive, and reusable workflow dependencies, closing the gap between code review and actual execution. The feature eliminates risks from tag movement and maintains a single source of truth for dependency versions.
content:
A moving tag is not a review


Your workflow can keep saying uses: vendor/build-action@v3 while the code behind v3 changes. That leaves a gap between the commit your team reviewed and the commit a later workflow run actually executes. Pinning every action by hand to a full commit SHA narrows that gap, but it is easy to miss transitive dependencies and reusable workflow calls.
GitHub Actions workflow dependency lockfiles are now in public preview for Free, Team, and eligible Enterprise Cloud plans. The GitHub CLI extension gh actions-lock generates .github/workflows/actions.lock; GitHub says an onboarded workflow must have its dependencies represented there, and runs use the recorded commits even if a tag or branch moves. The file records direct actions, transitive action dependencies, and reusable-workflow dependencies. GitHub’s October 14 announcement also describes gradual onboarding, stale-lock checks, policy enforcement, and Dependabot updates. The preview is useful for teams whose review process already depends on knowing exactly what automation code will run, but a lockfile does not tell you whether the locked code is trustworthy. GitHub’s announcement explains the current preview scope and behavior.
A workflow reference such as owner/action@v3 is readable, but a tag is a name that can be moved. A full commit SHA in the workflow pins that one reference directly. The lockfile takes a different approach: your workflow can retain a human-meaningful ref while the generated lock records the exact commit to use. For an onboarded workflow, GitHub requires the needed lock entries and executes the locked commit.
That is most valuable when a workflow uses more than one action or when actions themselves call other actions. The lockfile captures those transitive dependencies too, so your review can see the resolved set rather than relying on each top-level action tag. If your app asks a large language model a yes-or-no question, you have probably lived through this: you request a clean label, the model replies with a paragraph, and somewhere in your codebase a regular expression tries to drag the word "refund" out of "I believe this does constitute a refund request." It works on Monday. By Friday the model is feeling chatty, the regex misses, and a support ticket goes to the wrong queue.
On 6 October, OpenAI put a public beta of a different answer in front of developers: the Decisions API, a new endpoint — POST /v1/decisions — that returns typed verdicts instead of prose. No paragraphs to parse, no JSON mode to coax, just a probability, a choice, or a score. This is a practical guide: what the endpoint does, what it costs, where it genuinely helps, and the calibration work it quietly leaves to you.
The idea is deliberately narrow. You send evidence (input) plus one or more questions, and the API answers each question in a fixed shape. Three question types exist:
Predicate — a yes-or-no condition, answered with a probability between 0 and 1. "Does this photo show visible product damage?"


Choice — a fixed set of candidate answers you define, answered with the winning choice, the option probabilities and a confidence value. "Which department owns this ticket?"


Score — an ordered rubric you define, answered with a probability-weighted average across the levels, plus a confidence. "How severe is this incident?"

title: I Burned 95% of My AI Coding Quota in 2 Days — Here's What the Logs Revealed
summary: Analysis of three days of Claude Code usage revealed 99.9% of tokens were context re-reads and 97.6% were cached material; long sessions with growing context and parallel subagents amplified token costs dramatically. Breaking work into focused sessions, reducing parallel review cycles, and using smaller models for routine tasks can cut consumption by 75%.
content:
I use Claude Code every day to build a SaaS product. This week, the usage meter hit 95% before Wednesday. I assumed I had somehow written a mountain of code.
I hadn't.
Every request is logged locally, so I added it up. Here's what three days of work looked like (October 12–15):
65,000 requests
12.6 billion tokens processed
14 million tokens of actual output
That means 99.9% of my tokens weren't code. They were the model re-reading what it already knew.
97.6% of all tokens were cache reads. Every turn, the agent resends the entire conversation so far: files read, tool results, earlier decisions.
When the context sits at 200k tokens, a one-line reply still costs 200k tokens of reading.
Two thirds of my volume came from requests with more than 200k tokens of context. Only 2.5% came from requests under 50k.
A long session doesn't cost more because it does more. It costs more because every new turn is more expensive than the last.
My workflow splits work into small tasks. For each task, one subagent implements and two review — one for spec conformance, one for code quality. It produces clean results.
It also produced 78% of my requests and 53% of my tokens.
Each subagent starts with a fresh but still large context, runs many tool calls, and each call re-reads that context. One task becomes dozens of requests.
Out of 46 sessions, five accounted for three quarters of the total volume. These were multi-hour runs where the context kept growing and I never started over. One of them averaged almost 400k tokens of context per request.

title: Understanding Solar Street Light Installation Layouts
summary: Solar street light installation requires choosing between single-side, double-side (opposite or staggered), center-median, and cable-suspension arrangements, each suited to different road geometries and coverage requirements. The appropriate layout depends on road width, pole height, and desired lighting uniformity rather than any universal optimal configuration.
content:
Solar street light installation is not just about choosing a suitable lamp and mounting it on a pole. The arrangement of the lights along a road also affects lighting coverage, uniformity, and the overall design of a project.
Several common layouts are used in road lighting. Each has different requirements depending on road width, pole height, available space, and the desired lighting distribution.

Single-Side Arrangement
In a single-side arrangement, all light poles are installed along one side of the road.
This layout is often considered for narrow roads, access roads, and smaller streets where one-sided installation can provide sufficient coverage. However, the road width, mounting height, and light distribution must be evaluated carefully to avoid uneven illumination on the opposite side.
Double-Side Arrangement
Double-side arrangements place poles along both sides of the road. Two common configurations are used.
Opposite arrangement: Poles on both sides face each other at similar positions. This can provide a more balanced lighting pattern across the road.
Staggered arrangement: Poles alternate between the two sides rather than lining up directly opposite each other. This may help distribute light more evenly along the road, depending on the luminaire's optical design and pole spacing.
Neither configuration is automatically better. The appropriate choice depends on the road geometry and the required lighting performance.
Center Arrangement
In a center arrangement, light poles are installed along the central divider or median of a road, with luminaires positioned to illuminate the required areas on either side.
This layout may be suitable for divided roads and wider road sections where a central installation is practical. Pole structure, mounting height, and luminaire orientation must be designed to provide adequate coverage in both directions.
